summary: For ages 5–7, teach temperature as how hot or cold something is, that a thermometer is the tool that measures it, and the use of hot/warm/cool/cold to describe how the air feels on different days. Keep observation relative and qualitative (warmer/cooler/about the same), not exact °C. This is a design choice that stays within the K-ESS2-1 assessment boundary, which limits quantitative observations [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-ESS2-1]. Ground the word in felt experience first, then connect that sensation to a thermometer's reading rising when warmer and falling when cooler, and build hot–warm–cool–cold as one continuous scale rather than two opposite boxes.
misconceptions: 'Hot and cold are opposite THINGS' rather than points on one temperature scale — build the continuum (warm and cool are in between).
'What feels colder IS colder' — metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature; sensation is an unreliable exact measure (that's why we use a thermometer).
'The thermometer makes/adds heat' or controls temperature — it only measures and reports it.
'Higher number = the thermometer is bigger/fuller of liquid, not hotter' — tie the rising column explicitly to warmer.
'Temperature and weather are the same thing' — temperature is one PART of the weather, alongside rain, wind, cloud.

activities.title: Warm it up, cool it down: watch the thermometer respond
steps: Start from a plain scene with a large friendly thermometer beside it whose coloured column can rise and fall against a hot–warm–cool–cold band (no fine °C scale).
Warm the scene (e.g. drag the sun high into the sky, brighten the day) and watch the thermometer's column climb up onto 'warm', then 'hot'.
Cool the scene (slide the sun behind a cloud, or move the character and the thermometer into the shade) and watch the column sink lower, toward 'cool'.
Drop everyday things onto a shelf — an ice cube, a mug of cocoa, a cool drink — and touch the thermometer to each one to see it read lower or higher for each.
Line those things up coldest to hottest, and compare 'today vs yesterday' as higher or lower on the same thermometer.
Say in words whether each change made it warmer or cooler, and how the thermometer showed it.
activities.insight: Temperature is how hot or cold something is, it can be ordered along one scale from cold to hot, and a thermometer is a tool that reports it — the reading moves up when warmer and down when cooler, so 'higher means warmer.'

activities.title: Feel first, then name it
steps: Hold or look at things that are clearly warm, cool or cold (a warm drink, an ice cube, a sunny spot, cool shade) and say how each feels.
Match felt-experience cards — ice cube, warm drink, cool shade, hot sand — to the words hot, warm, cool, cold.
Order familiar places as a scale: freezer → fridge → room → warm bath, from coldest to hottest.
Decide for the air outside today whether it feels hot, warm, cool, or cold.
activities.insight: The word 'temperature' names a sensation children already know, and warm and cool are the in-between points between hot and cold — it is a continuum, not two boxes.

activities.title: Label the thermometer and compare two days
steps: Explore a labelled thermometer: tap or point to the bulb, the coloured column, and the scale to learn the parts.
Open a 'higher = warmer' flap or prompt that explains which way the reading moves when it gets warmer.
Look at paired scenes — a sunny beach and a frosty morning — and say which thermometer reads higher and why.
Describe in your own words what the thermometer does: it measures and reports how hot or cold it is; it does not make heat.
activities.insight: A thermometer has parts (bulb, column, scale), it reports temperature rather than creating it, and a higher reading means warmer.

activities.title: Coldest-to-hottest ordering check
steps: Order a set of everyday things from coldest to hottest.
Match an object to the right temperature word (ice → cold, warm drink → warm, and so on).
Use a relative-position slider to set the thermometer 'warmer than the fridge' or 'cooler than a warm bath' without using exact degrees.
activities.insight: Temperature items can be placed in order along one scale, and relative language (warmer than / cooler than) describes positions on that scale.

activities.title: Warmer or cooler than yesterday? Talk it through
steps: Respond to a prompt such as 'Is it warmer or cooler than yesterday, and how do you know?'
Give the comparison in words and the reason (how it feels, or what the thermometer shows).
Connect the thermometer reading to the daily weather routine — check today against yesterday.
activities.insight: Comparative temperature language (warmer/cooler/about the same) describes how one day differs from another, tying the instrument to lived weather.

activities.title: Same room, same temperature: feel versus measurement
steps: Leave a metal object and a wooden or plastic object side by side in the same room for at least an hour, away from sunlight, heaters and draughts.
Feel both, then predict what a thermometer will read on each — and say your reason BEFORE measuring.

With an adult, measure both by holding the same contact thermometer probe firmly against each object until the reading stops changing (do not use an infrared thermometer on shiny metal, which can read wrongly low), then compare the readings with your prediction.
Discuss: 'If both sat in the same room all morning, could they really be different temperatures?' and 'Which do you trust more to tell you the temperature — your hand or the thermometer?'
Try the follow-up: put the metal object in the fridge and leave the wooden one out, then measure both and say what changed.
activities.insight: How something feels is not a reliable measure of its temperature: things that have sat together in the same room for long enough, away from sun and heaters, end up at about the same temperature even if the metal feels colder, because metal draws heat from your hand faster. A thermometer measures the object or air, not your sensation.

checkQuestion: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have both been sitting on the same table in the same room all morning. Sam touches them and says the metal one is colder, so it must be at a colder temperature. If we put a thermometer on each, what would it read, and why?
checkAnswer: The thermometer would read the SAME temperature for both, because they have been in the same room all morning — both are at room temperature. The metal only FEELS colder to your hand; how something feels isn't a reliable way to know its temperature, which is why we use a thermometer.
